397.t: First night with Dizzy: no English, hand signals and known repertoire
397.s: With Jerry Gonzalez translating, Dizzy gives hand signals for swing, 6/8 and solos, and Berroa knows the tunes.
397.q: My English was zero. Actually it’s a funny part of the story, when Mario called me and he gave me the address and the instructions, I asked him, “Well Mario, you’re going to go with me, you’re going to be there, right?” Because I don’t speak English so how am I going to communicate with Dizzy? And…

397.t: Why Dizzy chose him: bebop with Afro-Cuban elements
397.s: Mario Bauza recommended him to Dizzy, who wanted to fuse Afro-Cuban rhythms with jazz.
397.q: Well yes. I think that, I’m sure that was the key. This was a guy that was always looking for new things. He was the guy that, by the suggestion of the great Cuban musician Mario Bauza, he hired [gap] 39:25 so he saw something in me obviously, that showed us [gap] he saw a guy that had the…

397.t: The no-audition first night at Fat Tuesday
397.s: Called by Mario Bauza as emergency replacement, he got hand signals from Dizzy and played tunes he knew.
397.q: No. No, no, no, no, no, no. He was, one day he had an engagement in New York. He was desperate looking for his drummer because his favorite drummer wasn’t able to leave Boston because they shut down the city due to a snowstorm and Dizzy had an engagement at a club in New York at Fat Tuesday. So…

328.s: He joined Dizzy's band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson and Melba Liston, mostly learning, and wrote later for the United Nations band.
328.q: Well I’ll tell you, we have to look at that. Because I joined Dizzy’s band in either the late fifties or the early sixties. And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head…

328.t: Leaving Ferguson for Dizzy's big band
328.s: He joined Dizzy's big band with Benny Golson, Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly and Melba Liston, learning a lot.
328.ch: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
328.q: Yeah, with Dizzy’s big band. That band was way over my head, but I had to go there anyway. Benny Golson was there, and Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly. Melba Liston was the musical director. I had to go there. I had to go there and get kicked, kicked and beat-up on. I did it. They taught me a lot in there.

328.s: Melba Liston was Dizzy's musical director and arranger and was treated with respect.
328.ch: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
328.q: Yes it was. I didn’t know that she was as heavy musically as she was. I got in that band. I learned it real fast. Musically, she was heavy.

553.s: Gillespie sends for him in 1948 to replace James Moody; he stays about two years.
553.ch: Road bands and the Gillespie band
553.q: ...musicians, we would get up and study our instrument, our craft–music–how we could excel. That was the art of the day, and this went on for years. Uh finally, in ’48 uh the Dizzy Gillespie band returned from Europe without James Moody, who had just had a, just hit Moody’s Mood For Love.

553.t: Learning Gillespie's conducting cues in the big band
553.s: How he learned to hold notes until Gillespie's arm dropped, a way of phrasing that cannot be written down.
553.ch: Road bands and the Gillespie band
553.q: Uh okay, um that was a learning experience for me. Uh for example...uh maybe the first two weeks I was in the band, we would play arrangements like Swedish Suite, Jump Did-Le Ba, and...I would, I would get to an end of a phrase in, in the saxophone section, and like the last note say is a whole…

553.t: Gillespie band personnel and the Afro-Cuban repertoire
553.s: He names the sidemen and writers in the band and the Afro-Cuban pieces still played after Chano Pozo's death.
553.ch: Road bands and the Gillespie band
553.q: ...the third alto player, John Brown, first [alto saxophone]. Um...uh there was [James] “Hen Gates” [Forman] on piano, Willie Kirk on trumpet. Um...Al McKibbon on Tape 1, 33:09-35:26 bass, [Louis] “Sabu” Martinez, conga drum. Um...Lamar Brothers[?] on trumpet, uh J.J. Johnson on trombone, Sam Most,…

114.s: He recalls the band personnel and that he did not realize what he was part of.
114.q: But you see what I’m saying though? And like if a kid sees something, and you show it to him, and he can do it slowly, and — oh, I see that. It’s simple. They call it the light bulb going on. And I always say this, like I’ve been kind of fortunate, because if I explain something to you this way and…

114.t: Arrangers for Dizzy and what he learned from Dizzy
114.s: Gil Fuller and Gerald Wilson wrote the arrangements; a flat five story; Dizzy's lessons keep surfacing; the phone number anecdote.
114.q: Gil Fuller. Walter Fuller. Walter Fuller did the arrangements and then after a while I think Gerald Wilson did a couple of things. I never will forget because Gerald Wilson did something, and this chord kept coming up. I said, “Diz” I said, “hey man, that’s wrong, that’s wrong, man, that note’s…

555.t: Finding Dizzy's band at 49th Street, borrowed trombone
555.s: Searching for the club by subway she found Dizzy's chair had been empty a week; she had to rent a trombone and wear a borrowed uniform in the band with Coltrane.
555.q: I went, and Dizzy found a spot for him to go, but that was in the wintertime. [She cannot remember the name of the club.] I didn’t know how to get there. Gerald was out of town. I had finished my work. I said, damn, I got to get to see Dizzy. I don’t want to have to sit down here and do nothing. So…

555.t: Back to Dizzy in New York and the audience's reaction
555.s: Dizzy sent for her again about 1949; the musicians were cool but audiences were surprised at a woman trombonist, and Wilson had introduced her as a complete musician.
555.q: No, I wasn’t unhappy. I just – one day I said no. I quit that. Just me and music again. Then maybe Dizzy sent for me again.

64.t: Dizzy Gillespie's first 52nd Street band and the end of the Webster job
64.s: He ran between Webster and Dizzy's new group, sat in for the missing Bud Powell, and lost his Webster job when George Wallington was hired.
64.ch: New York scene and bebop community
64.q: Immediately because I’m now in a place where when I’m working with Ben Webster, Dizzy Gillespie starts with the Opens, with the first bebop band even to be on 52nd Street. Now I’m playing with Ben, and he opens without a piano player because Bud Powell is supposed to be the piano player. The groups…

64.s: He describes the all-star big band, its ragged ensemble work and the renaming from Dream Band to Symphony Sid and Birdland.
64.q: And Dizzy’s book was hard, there was hard stuff in that book. So guys are scuffling. Some of them had not done a lot of big band playing and others just didn’t care to do a lot of big band playing. It was ragged. It sounded horrible, the ensemble. As soon as anyone took a solo, it was magic but the…

19.t: No drummer, and a book of eight arrangements, some rejected by Basie
19.s: Max Roach and Shadow Wilson are unavailable, a white drummer fills in, and the band's few charts include rejects from Basie and Dizzy's Night in Tunisia.
19.q: And during the wartime situation, all musicians were hard to find. We were fortunate to get these people. We had hoped to have either Max Roach or Shadow Wilson with the band, but somebody had scooped both of them up. I think Max Roach was with Benny Carter at that particular time, and I don't know…

19.t: First dance in Wilmington: Dizzy as straw boss and head arrangements
19.s: Dizzy runs the band, calling blues choruses for Malachi and riffs for the sections, and Eckstine asks all writers for charts.
19.q: Anyway, we went down, and we started the dance off that night with Dizzy... Dizzy was the straw boss of the band. he used to rehearse the band. So he'd come over to the piano and tell me to play a couple of choruses of the Blues, and he'd give me a tempo, and I'd play a couple of choruses, or as…

556.t: Visiting stars at the workshop and Dizzy taking his sidemen
556.s: Big-name players in town for Al Hirt's club visited the workshop; Cannonball's embrace confirmed their direction, and Dizzy Gillespie hired George Davis and David Lee. He argues New Orleans should be bombarded with modern jazz.
556.q: Well, fortunately at the time that the workshop happened, Al Hurd had a club on Bourbon Street that featured a lot of the name acts. And when serious musicians come to town, they kind of look for the places to go to hear differently. And we had gotten a pretty good reputation as jazz players. And…

158.t: Dizzy Gillespie's band and sitting in with Basie in Philadelphia
158.s: Dizzy breaks up his big band; Grey sits in with Basie when a trombonist is ill, fetches his horn, and is offered the England tour.
158.q: Yeah. I would dare so very strongly about that. Why because coming up with Dizzy doing things for the State Department and everything like that, we could begin to see these things. But coming on up into Basie, in which you know I spent almost 20 years of my life off and on with Basie, that’s a…

159.t: Dizzy's quintet personnel and salary on the road
159.s: Leo Wright and Les Spann in the group; recordings made; paid salary, on the road about 40 weeks a year.
159.ch: Going solo and the Dizzy Gillespie years
159.q: No, I wasn’t in the band with James Moody. I’ve played a lot of gigs with Moody, I sure wish he had been there. It was Leo Wright, an alto player that’s passed away also, a young alto player originally from Texas but he lived in Germany a great part of his life. He was stationed in the Army there.…

557.t: Joining Dizzy Gillespie after growing up near his family
557.s: Roker knew Gillespie's family in Philadelphia, was heard by him while working with Lee Morgan, and spent nine years in his band.
557.q: Now that was an experience for me I mean that will last me all my life. I’m from Philadelphia. Now I lived at 12th and Catharine. And Dizzy’s mother lived in the 1300 block of Catharine Street. So I’d been seeing Dizzy Gillespie, because he has a nephew that he took care of. You know his brother…

494.s: Moody tells him Lalo Schifrin is leaving; Dizzy hires him unheard and he learns the book on the first gig.
494.ch: Dizzy Gillespie, Yusef Lateef and 1960s New York
494.q: Yeah. They were working at Birdland. I had just got married. They were working at Birdland. I just happened to run into Moody on Broadway. He mentioned to me that Lalo Schiffrin was leaving the band and asked me if I would be interested. Are you kidding? Of course. So I went down to Birdland to…

503.t: Illinois Jacquet's offer and first recordings with Dizzy Gillespie
503.s: His mother refused the Jacquet job; at nineteen he spent a month with Dizzy Gillespie, recording Tin Tin Deo and Birks Works.
503.ch: High school, Dizzy and Wayne State
503.q: had these jam sessions and the younger musicians could come in. Anyway, I was able to meet all kinds of musicians there; Clark Terry, Joe Jones, you name it. Illinois Jacquet, is one of them, and I remember he offered me a job to go on the road with him and he had a great band with Joe Newman and…

558.t: Auditioning for Dizzy Gillespie and the 'tomorrow' misunderstanding
558.s: Introduced by Catalino Rolon, he auditioned at the Downbeat with Billy Taylor, misunderstood Dizzy's 'tomorrow', and was hired a year by Taylor before joining Dizzy.
558.ch: Jazz, Chano Pozo and Dizzy Gillespie
558.q: That was in 19 . . . well I met Dizzy in 1952, but Chano died in 1948. I met Dizzy in 1952 in one of the trips where I went and came in ‘52. There in . . . I was working in a Broadway show called Noche en la Habana, A Night in Havana. When I finished the show I went to the Palladium. The orchestras…

134.t: Gene Ammons, Billy Eckstine's band and the Chicago nucleus of Dizzy's band
134.s: They discuss Jug's path from Kolax to Eckstine and Red Top, and how Diz drew on Hines, Eckstine and Kolax alumni.
134.ch: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
134.q: And also I think that great trumpet player that ended up playing with my brother George. He was on Gene Ammons’s Red Top. Gail Brockman. All these cats had big names. Diz just – when he started that greatest band of the century, he more or less got them from Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine and King…

62.s: Wilson lists the personnel, including Coltrane, Jimmy Heath, Paul Gonsalves, Melba Liston, John Lewis, and the tour that ended when Dizzy went back to a small group.
62.ch: Lunceford, Ellington, Gillespie and the big bands
62.q: Yeah, okay. Paul Gonsalves is playing tenor. Al Gibson – Al Gibson, you know who Al was. Al played with Cab Calloway’s band. He was a fine um, baritone player. But Dizzy had played with Cab too you know, so he knew him from that. And that – that was us and oh yeah Jesse – Jesse Powell, another…

491.t: Joining Dizzy Gillespie's band, then his sextet
491.s: Quincy Jones called him to replace Ernie Wilkins in Gillespie's band, where hearing Dizzy up close depressed and inspired him; he later played in Gillespie's sextet with trombonist Silly Willy.
491.ch: New York, Bostic and Dizzy Gillespie
491.q: Can’t stand it any more. You’re killing me. So I got my money. I’m catching my flight from Seattle back to New York the next day. But early that morning, I got a call from Quincy Jones. “Benny. Ernie Wilkins is leaving the band, because he” – he’s going to write for Tommy Dorsey and all this stuff.…

135.t: Dizzy's sextet with Coltrane, Milt Jackson and a parade of drummers
135.s: Heath recalls joining Dizzy in 1950-51 alongside Coltrane, who was fighting addiction, and the many drummers who came and went.
135.q: Okay, before we can get to that though, I went on the road with Dizzy, with John Coltrane, Jimmy Heath, Milt Jackson. See, I had been playing with Milt Jackson almost my whole professional career ‘cause he was in that band with Maggie also. And the price wasn’t right for him to go to Paris, but we…

108.s: Wilder recalls trumpet section members Dave Burns, Lammar Wright Jr., Elmon Wright, Al McKibbon and Howard Johnson.
108.q: Dave Burns was in the trumpet section, Lammar Wright, Jr., Ike – I can’t think of his last name. There were several people who came. Elmon Wright was in the band at one time. Al McKibbon, the bass player, was with him. Who played piano? I’m trying to remember.

408.s: On Dizzy's band the music was memorized, as on a one-nighter in Boston with Wynton Kelly.
408.ch: Studio years and the 1959 Europe tour
408.q: jazz club up in Boston. But for some reason I remember we had um Al Haig was playing piano at that time with Dizzy’s band and we were hung up … we were all on the bus waiting to get up to go to Boston and Al was having union problems, and Dizzy’s waiting and we’re waiting and waiting and waiting…

374.t: Losing the Cubana Be score in a taxi
374.s: He left the score of Cubana Be, Cubana Bop in a taxi, and Gil Fuller rebuilt it from the recording.
374.ch: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
374.q: I think he had the recording, and from the recording he made – from the recording of the Carnegie Hall thing, the guys had the music. They already had the music. It’s just the score that got lost. He had time. He had a lot of time then to listen.

123.t: Billy Eckstine's band at the Regal Theater
123.s: He recalls Eckstine's band with Miles Davis and Doug Mettome, plus altoist Flap Dungee, in its last week.
123.q: It’s funny, he had at the Regal, he had an alto player that played like in Bird’s old Kansas City swingin’ style. His name was Flap - John Dungee - and he used to wear his saxophone strap over his shoulder instead of around his neck, and he sort of played like that. And he was just swinging and…

109.t: John Lewis's "Bright Lights" audition hires him on the spot
109.s: Clarke has Dizzy play Lewis's army-band arrangement, and Dizzy hired him on the spot to the arranging staff with Walter Fuller.
109.q: Eckstine, and everybody would laugh. So when John came to New York, I said, "That's fine. That works out just great, because I'm on my way to rehearsal. Why don't you pass by and pick me up, and I'll give you my address and we'll go together." So he shows up and we go. I said, "Bring that music we…

113.t: Playing Don Redman's booked dates when bookings ran short
113.s: When bookings fell short, the band played dates sold as Don Redman's, with Redman waving the baton while they played their own book.
113.ch: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
113.q: We was speaking about the band carrying themselves. One time, the -- well, our bookings was running real short. So we took some dates that the little short guy, you know who I'm talking about, that arranged so -- you know, and he also used to write for the Chesterfield Band.

166.t: Billy Eckstine's band personnel and substituting at the Plantation
166.s: He lists band members and describes soaking his hands in alum to substitute for Tommy Potter.
166.ch: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
166.q: Anyway, after Earl Hines' band, then Billy Eckstine formed a band, and he got all of the stars, you know. And he had -- at one time, he had -- let's see, in the reed section he had Dexter Gordon, Budd Johnson, Little Johnny Jackson -- I can't remember who the other one was. And in the trumpet…

90.t: Joe Morris' Plantation and the Eckstine band again
90.s: The Plantation at 97th and Central, and the Eckstine band's new personnel; Dizzy rehearsing 'Woody 'n You'.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: Also, out on the south end, around 97th and Central Avenue, they had a club that played big bands. And that's where I heard Billie Holiday again. It was called the Plantation. The owner's name was Joe Morris; it was called Joe Morris' Plantation. And when Billy Eckstine came to town with his band,…

91.t: Famous Door sextet with Jimmy Hamilton and Dizzy Gillespie
91.s: At the Famous Door he led a sextet with Hamilton and Gillespie, who he hired after hearing him with Calloway.
91.q: Yes. He'd been with Cab Calloway, and I liked what he was doing, and I asked him if he would join me ...

235.t: Ike Quebec recommends him to Dizzy
235.s: Ike Quebec declined Dizzy's offer and recommended Nicholas, whom he knew from Chicago; he met the band in Detroit.
235.ch: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
235.q: Ike Quebec. He wanted Ike Quebec, but Ike didn't want to go with the band so he told him about me. So Dizzy sent me a telegram.

529.t: Dizzy Gillespie's small band of the late fifties
529.s: Sam describes Dizzy's unrecorded small band with Sonny Stitt, Wynton Kelly, Jimmy Cobb and Candido.
529.q: Calling me from South America, you know. So I--after I quit that band, I didn't want no more of that. That was enough of that, man. My nerves was getting ready--then I went in Dizzy's band--Dizzy Gillespie--which was a fine band. This band was--oh, man, and we didn't record not one note. This band…
